extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (graduate students, researchers, and authors) preparing research papers and expository articles
extracted.subtask_description: Practical style and substance guidelines for writing mathematical research papers, covering logical clarity, structure, citation, LaTeX usage, and fine grammatical/notation choices. Intended to help authors produce clearer, less ambiguous, and more reader-friendly mathematics writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: (1) Explain what a claim follows from
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim does not follow immediately from the previous sentence alone, explain what it does follow from.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “Combining the previous two sentences shows that...”; “By Lemma 8.3, ...”.

rubrics_metrics.name: (2) Justify each claim in multi-claim sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: If a sentence contains more than one claim, make clear which reason is the justification for each claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a chain of equalities, indicate which reason explains which equality; place a reason before or after the chain or use align environment with a reason at the right of each line.

rubrics_metrics.name: (3) Ensure reader knows why each claim is true by the period
rubrics_metrics.description: A reader reaching the period of a sentence should know why each claim up to that point is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim's proof will come later, indicate this with language like “, as we now explain” or put the claim into a formal construction like a lemma followed by proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: (4) Eliminate ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not enough to write so that your words can be given the meaning you intend; write so that they cannot reasonably be given any other meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminate any ambiguity even if it would only cause a minute of confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: (5) Break up long arguments into lemmas
rubrics_metrics.description: Break up long arguments by making parts of them into lemmas, even if the lemmas are used only once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The goal is to minimize what a reader must keep in mind at one time.

rubrics_metrics.name: (6) State which results are used later
rubrics_metrics.description: If a section contains several theorems, propositions, and lemmas, but only one of them is needed in subsequent sections, mention this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioning this can free up the reader’s memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: (7) Make quantifiers unambiguous
rubrics_metrics.description: Make quantifiers unambiguous instead of writing ambiguous short forms like “We have x^2 + 1 ∈ S for x ∈ R.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write explicitly: “We have x^2 + 1 ∈ S for all x ∈ R.” or “We have x^2 + 1 ∈ S for some x ∈ R.”

rubrics_metrics.name: (8) Indicate where hypotheses are used
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs should usually indicate where the hypotheses are being used.

rubrics_metrics.name: (9) Include theorem/page numbers when citing
rubrics_metrics.description: When citing a book or article, include a theorem number or page number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit only when you really mean to cite the entire work.

rubrics_metrics.name: (10) Cite the published version when available
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite the published version instead of a preprint if the work has been published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: if citing a statement that exists only in the preprint version.

rubrics_metrics.name: (11) When citing arXiv include version/date
rubrics_metrics.description: When citing an arXiv preprint, include the version number or precise date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When citing a preprint elsewhere on the web, give the URL and manuscript date or date downloaded so readers can find the referred version.

rubrics_metrics.name: (12) Only cite forthcoming work if a public preprint exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite “forthcoming work” only if there is a publicly available preprint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: announcing unpublished forthcoming results can discourage others from working and may be damaging if the work does not appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: (13) Each part should describe the whole paper progressively
rubrics_metrics.description: The title, abstract, introduction, and body of an article should each describe the entire article, with each less abbreviated than the previous one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each should be written as if the reader will not look at what comes after.

rubrics_metrics.name: (14) Make titles specific and descriptive
rubrics_metrics.description: The title needs to be long enough to convey what the article is about, and specific enough to distinguish it from other articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague titles like “A class of polynomials.”

rubrics_metrics.name: (15) Omit filler phrases in titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit words such as “A note on” and “Remarks on” from the title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They add length without helping to describe the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: (16) Abstract should state main results if concise statements fit
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract should state the main results of the paper, if the statements can fit in a few lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions needed for precise statements are often omitted for space reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: (17) Abstract should be as self-contained as possible
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract should otherwise be as self-contained as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It should not contain citations or references to the body of the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: (18) Introduction should get to new theorems quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: The introduction to an article should get to new and interesting theorems as soon as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is OK to postpone definitions to a later Notation section if most readers can read the introduction without them; refer readers to that section when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: (19) Mathematics papers usually lack a conclusions section
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics papers usually do not have a conclusions section at the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: (20) Keep theorem statements short and define before use
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep theorem statements short. Definitions should precede the theorem in which they are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: (21) Keep sentences short
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep sentences short.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine sentences (with “, and” or a semicolon) only if it helps clarify logic or if the sentences are closely related.

rubrics_metrics.name: (22) String chains of equalities/inequalities together
rubrics_metrics.description: If an argument involves combining several equalities, string them together in one chain of equalities (in the correct order!) if possible; same for inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This uses transitivity and can make the logic easier to follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: (23) Do easier parts of broken proofs first
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proof breaks into parts, do the easier parts first.

rubrics_metrics.name: (24) When claiming isomorphism, specify the map
rubrics_metrics.description: When claiming that two objects are isomorphic, specify the map between them explicitly (at least one direction) and claim that that map is an isomorphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: (25) Start induction at base case 0 if easier
rubrics_metrics.description: Start induction arguments with base case n = 0 instead of n = 1 if it is easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: (26) Avoid writing “clear” without explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually when people write that something is “clear”, it is because they could not figure out a good explanation; if it really is clear, it is usually not necessary to say so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it is not clear, try to say a few words to give the reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: (27) Minimize “, where ...” constructions; define before use
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimize use of the “, where ...” construction where explanations of notation come after notation is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define variables before they are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: (28) Ensure sentence subjects are syntactic units, not split with formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject of a sentence or clause cannot consist of words outside a formula together with a fraction of the formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of splitting across lines, write the subject and predicate so the subject includes the whole variable/phrase, e.g., “For a quadratic polynomial a x^2 + b x + c, the discriminant Δ equals b^2 − 4ac.”

rubrics_metrics.name: (29) Introductory boilerplate before theorems usually unnecessary
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not mandatory to introduce each theorem or proposition with a sentence like “We now prove the following proposition.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such sentences add nothing; explanatory text about meaning/purpose can be useful though.

rubrics_metrics.name: (30) Avoid abbreviations like WLOG, iff, s.t.
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use abbreviations like WLOG, iff, and s.t.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those are appropriate for blackboard use only, if at all.

rubrics_metrics.name: (31) Avoid logical symbols ∃, ∀ outside formal logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use logical symbols such as ∃ and ∀ unless writing about formal logic where they appear in a logical formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write out “there exists” / “there exist” instead. See CMOS 12.5.

rubrics_metrics.name: (32) Do not start a sentence with a symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not start a sentence with a symbol; for example, avoid entire sentences like “H denotes the Sylow p-subgroup of G.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbols starting sentences are discouraged (see CMOS 12.7).

rubrics_metrics.name: (33) Avoid contractions in formal writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid contractions such as “don’t” in formal writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: (34) Prefer direct proofs over contradiction when equally easy
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use a proof by contradiction when a direct proof would be just as easy.

rubrics_metrics.name: (35) Refer to theorems by number, not position
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to theorems by number instead of writing “the previous theorem”, “the proposition above”, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: (36) Use single numbering system for theorem-like environments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a single numbering system for all theorems, lemmas, etc., instead of having overlapping numbers in the same paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
This makes statements easier to find and prevents citation errors; example LaTeX setup given using 
ewtheorem with shared counter (assumes amsart or amsthm).

rubrics_metrics.name: (37) Declare math operators in LaTeX
rubrics_metrics.description: To get proper typesetting for operators like Gal, put \DeclareMathOperator{\Gal}{Gal} once in the preamble and use \Gal in the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presumes amsart or appropriate package such as amsmath.

rubrics_metrics.name: (38) Use \hfill before enumerate to prevent misalignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Use \hfill before \begin{enumerate} if necessary to prevent misalignment of the first item in labeled theorem parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example shown for Theorem with (a), (b), (c) items.

rubrics_metrics.name: (39) Use \colon for maps in LaTeX
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of f : X \to Y, use f \colon X \to Y for appropriate spacing in LaTeX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare spacing differences in typeset output.

rubrics_metrics.name: (40) Consider fullpage package to fit more on a page
rubrics_metrics.description: Try \usepackage{fullpage} in the preamble to fit more on a page without setting margins manually.

rubrics_metrics.name: (41) Use microtype to reduce bad line breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Try \usepackage{microtype} just before \begin{document} to allow LaTeX to adjust spacing between characters and reduce bad line breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: (42) Consider colonequals package for := notation
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have mastered everything else, try \usepackage{colonequals} and use \colonequals as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare appearances of := and \colonequals carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: (43) Distinguish “so that” (purpose) vs “such that” (condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The words “so that” convey purpose, whereas “such that” imposes a condition; each instance of “so that” should be replaceable by “in order that” or “with the result that”.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good vs bad examples provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: (44) For logical implication write “A, so B”
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are indicating a logical implication between A and B, write “A, so B” instead of “A, so that B” or “A, and so B”.

rubrics_metrics.name: (45) Use semicolon/colon correctly to join sentences; adverbs don't change punctuation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Two sentences can be connected by a semicolon, not just a comma; a colon can be used if the second is an explanation of the first. Inserting adverbs like “therefore”, “hence”, and “thus” does not change this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “A, hence B” is wrong; “A, so B” and “A; therefore B” are correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: (46) Place “only” close to the word it modifies
rubrics_metrics.description: The word “only” should be placed as close as possible to the word it is modifying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Kil07 for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: (47) Use full noun phrase when introducing variable elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of “Given g an element of G” write “Given an element g of G”.

rubrics_metrics.name: (48) “Let” should be followed by the variable being defined
rubrics_metrics.description: What follows “Let” should be the variable being defined: e.g., instead of “Let the center of G be Z.” write “Let Z be the center of G.”

rubrics_metrics.name: (49) Capitalize the word “Theorem” when referring by number
rubrics_metrics.description: When referring to a theorem (or proposition or section...), capitalize the word “Theorem”.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “By Section 3.4 and Theorem 5.6, ...” and “By Faltings’s theorem, ...”

rubrics_metrics.name: (50) Maintain punctuation when displaying formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Displaying a formula does not change required punctuation; punctuation should appear as in running text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: “By Theorem 3.2, we have” then display and end with a period after the displayed formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: (51) Use “Assume that” for clause beginnings unless noun unit
rubrics_metrics.description: Use “Assume that G is a finite group.” rather than “Assume G is a finite group.”; exceptions allowed when the following phrase is a noun unit like Hypothesis A or n ≥ 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same rules apply to “Suppose”. See [Wes15] for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: (52) Use 1980s not 1980’s
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to the 1980s, not the 1980’s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See CMOS 9.34.

rubrics_metrics.name: (53) Follow punctuation convention for i.e. and e.g.
rubrics_metrics.description: I.e. and e.g. should be followed by a comma, at least in American English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If what comes before and after are full sentences, the i.e. or e.g. should be preceded by a semicolon instead of a comma.

rubrics_metrics.name: (54) Minimize parentheses; omit when traditional
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimize use of parentheses; for instance log x is better than log(x), and omit parentheses in traditional expressions like sin 2x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But in expressions like sin(x + y) parentheses are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: (55) Usually no centered dot for multiplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually it is not necessary to use a centered dot or other symbol for multiplication; write (n + 1)(n + 2) rather than (n + 1) · (n + 2) or ×.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If both factors are numbers, juxtaposition is confusing, so write 3 · 7.

rubrics_metrics.name: (56) Omit filler phrases like “We remark that” unless needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Filler words like “We remark that” and “Note that” should be omitted, except when their absence would produce a sentence starting with a symbol.

rubrics_metrics.name: (57) No need to state proof conclusion if QED symbol present
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proof ends with an end-of-proof symbol, it is not necessary to write “This concludes the proof.” or “Thus we are done.”

rubrics_metrics.name: (58) Use slash for fractions in exponents/subscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Fractions in exponents or subscripts should use the slash instead of being stacked vertically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write x^{3/2}, not x^{3/2} stacked in a small vertical fraction (author shows typed as x3/2 vs stacked). See CMOS 12.47.

rubrics_metrics.name: (59) Use parentheses for tuples and sequence notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordered tuples should be written (2, 3, 5) instead of {2, 3, 5}; sequences should be written (a_i)_{i≥0} instead of {a_i}_{i≥0}.

rubrics_metrics.name: (60) Distinguish “principal” vs “principle”
rubrics_metrics.description: The word “principal” means “main”; the word “principle” means “rule” or “law”.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: principal results, principal ideal vs maximum principle, principle of mathematical induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: (61) Watch commonly misspelled math words
rubrics_metrics.description: Commonly misspelled words include separable (not seperable), archimedean (not archimedian), homogeneous (not homogenous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pronunciation note for homogeneous given.

rubrics_metrics.name: (62) Prefix “non” usually does not need hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: The prefix “non” does not need a hyphen when it appears in common words such as nonempty, nonnegative, nonsingular, nontrivial, and nonzero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See CMOS 7.85.

rubrics_metrics.name: (63) Most numbers in math papers should be numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Most numbers in math papers should be written as numerals instead of words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: single-digit numbers used only as counting numbers may be spelled out as words (e.g., “These two genus 2 curves...”); note some authors spell small numbers as words more often.

rubrics_metrics.name: (64) Prefer “since” over “as” when causal
rubrics_metrics.description: Technically it is OK to use “as” as a synonym for “since”, but this usage sounds stilted and can make sentences harder to parse; therefore prefer “since”.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of egregious use: “As x does not tend to +∞, the expression e^x is bounded.”

rubrics_metrics.name: (65) Do not use “per” when you mean “by”
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use “per” when what you mean is “by”.
